utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone. Case number IT-95-14-R77.2, the Prosecutor versus Ivica Marijacic and Markica Rebic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution, David Akerson. I'll be the lead attorney today. To my right is Rebecca Graham and Salvatore Cannata. They will be assisting. And our case manager is Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akerson. For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. My name is Marin Ivanovic and I shall represent Mr. Ivica Marijacic. I'm a member of the Croatian Bar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Kresimir Krsnik, I'm a member of the Croatian Bar and I'm going to conduct the Defence of Mr. Markica Rebic. I'm assisted here by our case manager, Ms. Koraljka Tomasic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsnik. At this time I would like to make sure the accused are following in the language they understand. Mr. Marijacic, do you follow the procedure in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you turn on the microphone, please. THE ACCUSED MARIJACIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow the proceedings

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marijacic. How about Mr. Rebic. Do you follow the procedure in the language you understand? THE ACCUSED REBIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a Pre-Trial Conference in the trial of Mr. Ivica Marijacic and Mr. Markica Rebic for contempt of the Tribunal, which is a crime within the inherent jurisdiction the Tribunal and punishable under Rule 77 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. According to the operative indictment, dated 14th of October, 2005, the allegations against Mr. Marijacic are that he knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice in three respects: By publishing the identity of the protected witness, the statement of the witness, and the fact that the witness had testified in non-public proceedings before the Tribunal. The allegations against Mr. Rebic are that he knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice in three respects: By disclosing the identity of a protected witness, the statement and transcript of the witness, and the fact that the witness had testified in non-public proceedings before the Tribunal. I have to note my monitor is gone. The Rule 77(E) of the Rules state that Rules in parts four to eight of the Rules shall apply mutatis mutandis to contempt proceedings. This would mean that the contempt proceedings do not necessarily require the same course of proceedings usually envisaged by the Rules. Accordingly, the Trial Chamber shall adopt a somewhat flexible approach, reflecting the fact that this case involves a single count of contempt of the Tribunal and that the trial can be concluded in a relatively short period of time. Thus, as the parties are well aware, we have scheduled trial proceedings for two days; today, directly following this Pre-Trial Conference, and tomorrow. So I'd like to make sure to the parties that it is the Chamber's intention to conclude the trial proceedings within this period of time. With the foregoing in mind, this Pre-Trial Conference shall serve to narrow down the main issues of contention between the Prosecution and Defence so that we can focus the evidence and legal arguments on them during trial. Before going into these main issues, let me briefly discuss the conduct of the trial. The Trial Chamber is of the view that we will not have opening statements but, rather, commence with legal arguments following the Pre-Trial Conference, and then we'll have the Prosecution's case, to be followed by the Defence case. As for Defence case, I understand that both accused will give evidence as witnesses. I will leave it to the Defence who shall begin first. Since the accused will be giving evidence as witnesses, they shall make the solemn declaration pursuant to Rule 90, and their testimony shall not be considered as statements of the accused pursuant to Rule 84 bis. And at the end of hearing, a brief period of time shall be reserved for a brief closing remark from both parties. Before we hear from the parties on legal arguments, I'd like to -- I have to remind both the parties that as of yesterday, 16th of January, 2006, the Appeals Chamber issued a decision on Prosecution's motion for variance of protective measures, lifting all protective measures granted with respect to Johannes Van Kuijk in the hearing of 16th of December, 1997 in the Blaskic case, and stating that the fact that witness Van Kuijk testified, his statement to the Prosecution, as well as his testimony transcript in Blaskic case may be referred to publicly and in open session. Furthermore, with regard to the first order of -- what was the date of -- sometime in June. With regard to the first order, the Appeals Chamber found that because protective measures were ordered out of the Trial Chamber's extreme concern for the security of witnesses residing in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, the Prosecution has failed to establish that those protective measures are applicable to witness Van Kuijk given that he testified that he was a Dutch army officer of the infantry stationed for a specific period of time in Central Bosnia. So before we hear from the Prosecution on their legal arguments, can I hear from Mr. Akerson what, if any, the Prosecution's position on this finding of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd first like to point out that we just received this at 6.00 p.m. last night and I was able to provide it to Defence counsel a few minutes ago, so they really haven't had a chance to look at it. I don't know if you want to give them a little bit of time to try to digest this order before you have a discussion on its application, or do you want me to go ahead and just render what our opinion is about this order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, can I ask you directly whether the Prosecution still needs to bother to prove that Mr. Rebic was representative of the Blaskic team, Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I -- it was never our position that that was a critical element that we had to prove in order to convict Mr. Rebic. It helps to establish the application of the 1997 order, but there's two provisions -- the June 1997 order. There's two provisions in that order in which the Blaskic Trial Chamber sought to stop the disclosure of protected witness information. One is that provision where they are directing it at the defendant, Mr. Blaskic, himself, his legal representatives -- his legal counsel and their representatives, but then there's another provision where they say that anyone who receives copies of the statements shall be instructed by the attorneys and Defence counsel not to reproduce them under pain of contemptive sanction. And what was submitted in the motion to modify the protection measures was only submitted on the basis of the first clause, so I think the second clause still applies. That would be the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Appeals Chamber should have read all the text of the first order. Is it not clear from the reading of the Appeals Chamber decision that the first order of June 1997 is not applicable to this case? Do you not agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: We don't agree with that. The ruling of the Appeals Chamber, based on our interpretation -- that's certainly a reasonable interpretation of the Appeals Chamber's order. The other interpretation would be that they have said that, based on our submission in that motion, the Prosecution has failed to prove, based on that provision -- because that's the only provision they specifically mention, which is the witness Van Kuijk, we didn't establish that the first provision of -- of the 1997 order applied because he wasn't a resident of the former Yugoslavia and he was not personally -- and/or he was not personally -- the arguments put in favour of proceeding in closed session were not based on his personal safety. We still think there's an argument that, because what the Appeals Chamber said is that we didn't prove it for the purposes of that motion, that we could adduce evidence which would establish it and would allow us to go forward with the 1997 order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy has some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, the order in question was made because a previous order appeared to extend only to persons residing in Central Bosnia. So it was extended to the whole of the former Yugoslavia. And then if you read further on in the order, it says on page 6: "It therefore deems that the accused, his counsel, and their representatives must not disclose to the public or to the media the name of the witnesses from certain areas of the former Yugoslavia or any information which might make it possible to identify them unless that is absolutely necessary for preparing the Defence. The Trial Chamber also considers that additional measures must be implemented by both parties in order to guarantee satisfactory protection of the witnesses. It therefore orders the Prosecution and the Defence to ..." and then it goes on to deal with the second part you've just referred to. Now, is it not clear as day that that is simply a measure, an administrative measure to secure the effective implementation of the main order, which is to protect witnesses residing in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would submit is that the -- if you look at the order in its entirety, the Prosecution had originally requested a number of forms of relief, and that it could be interpreted that when the Blaskic Trial Chamber issued these orders that they -- they can be read individually, and so the order that I'm referring to orders the Prosecution and the Defence to instruct those persons who have received a copy of these statements not to reproduce them under pain of sanction can be read independently and it's still viable. That being said, if this Chamber wants to -- you know, it's not a critical part of this case, this 1997 order. I think it's a clear expression by the Blaskic Trial Chamber that they were making efforts to protect the closed-session testimonies that were being leaked in the newspapers. But the case doesn't turn on it. We haven't had a lot of time to digest the Appeals Chamber ruling, and I know the Defence counsel hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, it seems to me there might be a quite separate question whether any statement made by any witness has a degree of confidentiality that means it ought never to be divulged. However, you have never at any stage in this case suggested that that was a basis on which there might be contempt here. You've relied exclusively on the orders themselves and the general -- not perhaps exclusively on the terms of the orders but possibly also the spirit of the orders. But that's -- that's a separate question. It seems to me that on a pure and simple interpretation of this order, is confined to people residing in the former Yugoslavia, and that's the end of the matter as far as that order is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akerson. I wonder --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just respond very briefly to Judge Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: There is the issue of -- one of the complicating factors with all of these newspapers that have been disclosing confidential material is the confusion between a witness statement and his testimony, and at the juncture at which point a statement is actually released, because it seems to me that there is a point in time where when a witness testifies, even if you presume that witness statements at some point aren't protected at all, when a witness testifies in closed session and his witness statement covers the exact same material, which a lot of times it's at least going to be significantly overlapping, that by disclosing the witness statement after he's testified in closed session, the statement then assumes a cloak of protection, because when the Trial Chamber orders that a witness is entitled or needs to testify in closed session, they are protecting the content of what he's saying, at a minimum. The content of what he's saying also can be contained in the witness statement. So we would say that there is a timing question as to a witness statement, when protection may attach to it. At a very minimum. It may be that there's more protection of a witness statement than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll come to the issue of closed session, the effect of it, but can we confine our discussion on the first order of 6th of June, 1997, whether it is confined to those witnesses who were residing in the territory of former Yugoslavia and on a factual issue whether Prosecution is challenging that the witness Van Kuijk himself was residing in the former Yugoslavia or not. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No, we're not challenging the fact he was a member of the military. He was never a resident, in the legal sense, of the former Yugoslavia. He was residing in the former Yugoslavia on an interim basis or on a periodic basis as part of his duties, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akerson. I wonder if Defence has anything to say in relation to the first order and on what Appeals Chamber had said. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Our understanding of this is also very simple, and we believe that the decision of the Appeals Chamber and our position are very straightforward, as Judge Bonomy pointed out. It clearly transpires that protective measures, generally written as they are, are directed to the parties, et cetera, and generally refer only to the witnesses residing in the former Yugoslavia. It's very clear that they refer only to residents of the former Yugoslavia, and then the conclusion is very clear. If we are talking about a specific witness, Van Kuijk, this order had a general thrust and was more directed to some other witnesses whom I cannot mention because they still enjoy protection. They were not actually directed at witness Van Kuijk. This whole problem arose much, much later, in 2004; seven years later, after the entire Dutch Battalion had withdrawn. And if we talk about the reasons why anything was published in this Croatian newspaper at all, whatever was written could not have applied to a protected witness at all, because this witness never enjoyed such protection, let alone in 2004. That is our position, Your Honour, and it is clear in all our submissions. And we wanted ourselves to raise the first issue you began this discussion with, plus the issue whether Mr. Markica Rebic was indeed a member of the Defence team. I hope this issue will be resolved today. And in conclusion, I have to say it's very difficult for me to speak at this moment because it was only thanks to our learned colleague Mr. Akerson that I received this order of the Appeals Chamber only a few minutes before this hearing started, and we would be grateful for at least a couple of minutes in peace to read this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please try to do so. Yes, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, I would be very brief. We held the position from the very beginning that Mr. Marijacic never violated any orders of this Honourable Court. We believe it is very clear, especially now, that no portion of the transcript of the closed session was ever published. Hrvatski List newspaper never published --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Ivanovic. We'll come to the closed session order later on. We are discussing only the first order, whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but that is closely linked to the finding of the Court of the 6th of June, 1997, to the order of the 6th of June, which specifies that it refers to the parties in the courtroom. It has no other link with this case. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Prosecution's position is that while it is not challenging the fact that the witness Van Kuijk was not residing in the territory of former Yugoslavia, some parts of the first order of 6th of June in 1997 can be applicable to -- even to the witness who was not residing in the territory of former Yugoslavia. Am I correct in so understanding, Mr. Akerson? We are talking about the first order.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. That would be our position, that it's a general expression of the Blaskic Trial Chamber that is attempting to protect witnesses, and when -- when the two accused had knowledge of that order, that that extended even to Mr. Van Kuijk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, if the Trial Chamber did not decide that point now but left it to the trial, how would you be seeking to substantiate it, your argument, during the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Essentially through legal argument. One of the -- one of the cases cited by the Defence is a case out of the United Kingdom, the Levellee case, and one of the principles in that case is that contempt would apply in situations where the Court has made a clear expression of its intent to protect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to hear the argument now. I just wanted to be sure that you were seeking to do it through legal argument as distinct from witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And if I could just emphasise, this is a minor point in the case because the case really turns on closed session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you still need Mr. Tomljanovich as your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To prove that Mr. Rebic was part of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Not to prove that point, no. I don't need him for that point, and that was always a minor point of this case anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you wouldn't lead that evidence in trial, whether Mr. Rebic was a part -- representative of the Blaskic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. As suggested by Judge Robinson, the Chamber is of the view to leave the issue open 'til the later stage of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we shall come to the issue of second oral order for closed session. In relation to that, the Appeals Chamber said the following: "In its order, the Appeals Chamber noted that the reason why witness Van Kuijk's testimony was -- was ordered by the Trial Chamber to be conducted in closed session was not out of concern for witness Van Kuijk's own security but because he would be testifying about information that is extremely sensitive and because the questioning could intrude upon sensitive operational matters." Having said this, therefore one of the key issues in this case would be what if -- what the effect of such an order is, and I'd like to hear the legal submissions on this issue from the parties. And the third order -- in relation to third order, which ordered that publication of statements and testimony of the witness concerned and generally of any protected witness shall cease immediately. So same issue of the effect of the closed session, and the issue of whether the witness Van Kuijk was a protected witness at all rises here again. So we'll hear submission from the parties on this issue. But before I hear from you, Mr. Akerson, one issue that can possibly arise in relation to the third order is that while it is only the publication of statements or testimony that was prohibited by this order, it may be argued that Mr. Rebic is not alleged to have published anything and, therefore, cannot be alleged to have violated the order per se. Do you have anything to say? Start from this and continue your legal submissions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'll start with what Your Honour had first mentioned, which is the oral order, and that is when Mr. Van Kuijk appeared in front of the Blaskic Trial Chamber, there was a discussion as to whether or not he should testify in open session or closed session. The ruling was that he should testify in closed session. Very evident on the face of the transcript in a number of places that he was testifying completely in closed session. And it is the important principle that's at stake in this case. Mr. Van Kuijk testifies in closed session. His identity is never revealed in any part of open session. And assuming that the purpose of him testifying in closed session was to protect what he was testifying about and that the parties weren't concerned with protecting his identity, his identity was protected in closed session. And so this decision is going to define what the meaning of protection measures is, and it would be the Prosecution's position that the only reasonable interpretation is the simple interpretation that whatever is in closed session is protected. And in this particular case, Mr. Van Kuijk's identity was never revealed in open session. It was only mentioned in closed session and therefore it is protected and he is a protected witness. But a fundamental question for this case is what is a protected witness versus protection measures. The Appeals Chamber has said protection measures apply to this witness, and then the question is: Is he a protected witness or is he a witness who has protection apply to him? And it would be our position that because his identity was never revealed, that it opens a Pandora's box if you allow other people to go beneath the surface of a closed-session transcript and determine what the intent of the parties was and parse out what is protected and what is not protected. So our simple argument is he is a protected witness because his identity is never revealed outside of closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akerson, that's all very dramatic, but how is it you say that -- or are going to say that divulging the identity of the witness could have prejudiced the security of the material, which the Appeals Chamber have clearly stated was the purpose of that particular order? What you've said seems to me pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Our response would be, Your Honour, respectfully, that when the Blaskic Trial Chamber heard arguments that Mr. Van Kuijk should testify in closed session, they very well -- it's reasonable to come to the conclusion that they were only interested in protecting the content of what he said. But that's not what happened. Ultimately, Mr. Van Kuijk's identity was never revealed, and the record -- there's an ex parte motion filed by the Prosecution, and I think this Chamber's well acquainted that this argument is presuming that all the reasons to move into closed session were recorded on the record. But assuming that's the case, that everything was laid out and the Prosecution was never interested in protecting Mr. Van Kuijk's identity, his identity was protected because it was never revealed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you conceding that the Prosecution never aimed to protect his identity but aimed to protect the material?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I think that's -- from looking at the record, I think that's a fair analysis, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: But it would be our position - if I could just add one other point - it doesn't matter because his identity was never revealed. And if then subsequent parties, whether it be newspapers, anybody who happens to get a closed-session transcript, can look at a transcript and say, well, it's the intent of the parties only to protect this material, then it's my right to parse out what is protected and what isn't. It's a very dangerous precedent, because what that means, in this case the parties argued that they were concerned with Mr. Van Kuijk's operational details. He testifies in closed session to a lot of issues, and if this Chamber is considering adopting the position that someone can look at the intent of the parties in arguing for closed session and parse out that part of the closed-session testimony and publish closed-session testimony because the parties never advocated that that should be protected, then that's the Pandora's box and that's a dangerous precedent because then closed-session testimony really becomes subject to the argument the parties make as to why closed session should be imposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- I don't want to enter into a lengthy debate with you at this stage, but what that leaves out of account is the fact that the order -- the Rule clearly specifies that the reason for granting the protection must be stated on the record, and here it was clearly wasn't clearly stated but you can deduce what the reason was from the debate and from the terms of the transcript. Now, does that not rather nullify the submission you're making that if by coincidence the name never comes out, or if as a result of the order, even, the name never comes out, that somehow or other it's protected?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: It would be our position that it's a slippery slope, that unless we adopt a very simple interpretation of what closed session means, we're opening the door to really water down what a closed-session protection really affords, and if we allow parties to interpret based on the arguments, it's just going to become very complicated as to determine what protections really apply in these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder Mr. Akerson, you answered my question in relation to the third order, the order of 2000, which was concerned with the publication of statement or testimony, but Mr. Rebic was not alleged to have violated -- have published anything; he was alleged to have disclosed something. What is your view on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Our view would be that Rule 77(A)(ii) says that a person will be in contempt if they wilfully -- knowingly and wilfully interfere with the administration of justice, in this case by disclosing information relating to proceedings. He's charged in the indictment only with disclosing, not with publishing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that is related to the -- with the second order, not with the third order.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because third order is only concerned with publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, except for it -- in the -- on the face of the Hrvatski List article, there's an interview between Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic, and they are freely discussing that the purpose of him turning over this material is to have it published in the edition. So he is in essence participating in the publication of the material as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akerson. Before we come to the Defence, if the Defence wishes, the Chamber is minded to allow some time for the Defence to be able to read the decision of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. We do need a little time. But I would like first to respond very briefly, if you allow me, to the position of my learned colleague. The Defence believes to the contrary, that something else is a slippery slope; namely that the OTP of this Tribunal has much too great authorities and authorisations, some of them not completely justified, and they would like to stretch their confidentiality concerns to the entire globe. And of course civil law and our domestic law is familiar with witness protection, but their interpretation is, or seems to be that what is believed to be confidential by them may not be published anywhere around the globe. We all know that such an order on confidentiality can refer only to the parties to the proceedings; namely the Defence, the experts, anyone participating directly in the courtroom, people who may actually be aware of confidential, protected material. But what is the greatest concern to the Defence, Your Honour, is the fact that there is misrepresentation of the reasons why Van Kuijk received protection in the first place. Not because his security or his life were in danger; he received protection because the Dutch government asked for it. Why doesn't my colleague state this clearly? For military reasons, military reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He stated that clearly. He stated quite clearly that the Prosecution didn't even ask for protection for the witness's security. It went beyond that. It wasn't just that the Trial Chamber didn't grant it, he didn't -- his colleague didn't ask for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. And if protection was received, it was granted only to protect military concerns of the Dutch state. And the Dutch state started an initiative in 2005, citing Mr. Cameron, who will appear as a witness for the Prosecution, and they asked for all protective measures to be removed because all their concerns were now moot. Therefore, I believe that we cannot have such a unilateral, lopsided interpretation as my colleague seems to adopt. Only then would we be on a slippery slope, because one of the purposes, one of the goals of this Tribunal is to make public whatever can possibly be made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue that kind of debate, I take it from your submission that, Mr. Ivanovic, I assume you would not need Van Kuijk as a Defence witness any more, because all the issues have been resolved by the Appeals Chamber decision and by these legal submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is not the view of the Defence. It is not the view of the Defence that our party published anything from a closed session. We wanted witness Van Kuijk to confirm whether what was published in Hrvatski List was part of his statement or part of his testimony, whether what was published in Hrvatski List newspaper in any way endangered the concerns of the Dutch state. We would like to resolve now in the pre-trial stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but why do you need witness Van Kuijk himself to prove that what was part -- what was published in Hrvatski List was part of his statement? We can read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But who will confirm the authenticity of his statement? On the facts that was published in Hrvatski List newspaper, I cannot see that anyone signed the statement. I don't see who else I can call to confirm the authenticity of the statement. What I'm trying to say, Your Honour, is that of course if, when we study this decision, this decision of the Appeals Chamber, we will decide after giving it some more thought whether to call Mr. Van Kuijk or not, but what is important to say, I believe, is that all this time we see attempts -- we are witnessing attempts to link two distinct matters. Hrvatski List did not publish a single word from the closed-session testimony of witness Van Kuijk. That is very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is not the Prosecution's case that Hrvatski List published the closed-session testimony of Van Kuijk. Instead, it published a part of statements given to the Prosecution. It is clear from the indictment. And I thought it was the purpose of the Defence team to prove the fact that Mr. Van Kuijk was not residing in the territory of former Yugoslavia and that the protective was not given for his own security reason, so -- and those issues have been resolved. I don't think you need Mr. Van Kuijk any more. And I think this is the proper time to allow some time to allow the Defence to read the Appeals Chamber decision. Would a quarter of an hour be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. And I believe I can agree with your analysis. That is the crux of all our submissions and arguments from the beginning. Mr. Van Kuijk was not a protected witness. What was protected was his closed-session testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 15 minutes. --- Break taken at 9.55 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear from the Defence on the legal arguments. I hope you have had enough time to read the Appeals Chamber's decision. Mr. Ivanovic, will you start.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I should like to respond first of all to your question before the break. After we have reviewed the decision, we no longer intend to call Witness Van Kuijk as a witness in this case. As for the publication of the article, I think the position of the Appeals Chamber is very clear. They confirm almost all submissions of the Defence. First of all, the witness himself, Van Kuijk, was not a protected witness. It was his testimony that was protected for reasons of special interests of the OTP and the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The only thing that we take issue with in this case, and what we believe should be resolved before the trial, is the material itself, the material that is only a burden for this case. We have received over a hundred documents which have absolutely nothing to do with either the witness himself, Van Kuijk, or the accused who are present in this courtroom. Therefore, I believe that before we proceed with the trial a decision should be reached that the parties must focus on the charges -- on the charge of the indictment and not to introduce material which has nothing to do with the case against the accused. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. Mr. Krsnik, you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will be very brief. The position of the Defence of Markica Rebic is very clear. He was never a member nor was he able to be a member of the Defence team in the Blaskic case, the Defence which was led by Counsel Nobilo. As for the submissions, I think that was the submission that appeared for the first time at the last Status Conference, we received, and I believe you have, Your Honours, a pile of documents. I don't know how much time we will lose in order to prove this -- this allegation. That he was a member of the Defence team, I don't think I should waste my time on that. I think the position is clear. If you read the order of the Court, you will see that the -- his function was very clear. He was at the disposal of whoever needed any assistance from the Prosecution or from the Defence. He provided that assistance to both parties equally. Would that therefore mean that he was a member of the OTP of this Tribunal? No. I think my colleague went a bit too far, but I'm not going to waste precious time. I believe your decision will be fair and just. What concerns me, Your Honour, is that the witness that we intended to call, and you know who the witness is, if my colleague is going to maintain his position, I will have to call the witness. If not, I will then drop the witness. And I have been thinking of dropping other witnesses as well. We have another problem with this witness: He is sick. He has a 40 degree temperature, and I don't think he will be able to come. I fully agree with your positions, Your Honour, everything that you stated today, and the Defence is prepared to act as -- to be as flexible as possible today. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let me be clear about Mr. Krsnik. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: (redacted) Can we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, I apologise. That part can be redacted, if necessary. Can we go into private session, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At this time, the Chamber wishes to make sure that the witness's name should not be revealed in publications. Can I ask a question to the Defence that I leave it to you who will answer the question, but my understanding is that the Defence agrees that the testimony, not his -- his own security, his testimony is protected by the order of the closed session. That's what Mr. Ivanovic has said a minute ago. Then is the Defence position that the publication of his statement has nothing to do with that order? So, one, even if the witness, a certain witness gave evidence in closed session, it is free for anybody other than the parties to publish it at any time? Is it the Defence position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to be very cautious when trying to answer your question. I am inclined to agree that that should be a general principle. Not that everybody should be given such freedom but that it in every case we must be able to analyse who was given what kind of protection, because not all protective measures are identical, they're not all the same. There is a difference between a witness who comes to testify and who is from a destroyed village and comes to testify in a capacity of a victim and has his relatives and his friends who still live with him in the village in question. That situation is not the same as the protection given to a high-ranking officer of a high-level army which participated in a high-level mission involving NATO and other military forces and the purpose of such protection was to protect the interests of this armed force. These protective measures are not the same. Now, if the testimony of such an officer cannot be published, I don't know what we're talking about here. If within hundred years such protective measures are still in place, then nothing will -- no one will ever be able to publish that testimony which was given in closed session. What I'm saying -- my submission is that we have to look into the type and the reasons of specific protective measures afforded to individual witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Krsnik. Mr. Akerson, in terms of legal submission, do you have anything to add to what you have said earlier, and anything to respond to the Defence submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. In response to Mr. Krsnik's argument that he just made, it's clear from the way we do business, it's clear from the Appeals Chamber ruling that closed-session testimony is protected. Now, the issue, as I'm understanding it, is does that protection extend only to the transcript of that testimony or is the content protected? Because if a witness statement covers the exact same material, can a newspaper avoid contempt by saying we know this witness has protection measures, he testified in closed session, we're not going to print in our newspaper the transcript of his testimony, but we are going to print his witness statement that has the exact same material. So the question that this Court has to decide is the content of what the witness testifies to protected or is it literally the transcript? And I would say the only reasonable conclusion, the only reasonable interpretation is it has to be the content, because what that opens the door to is if a newspaper says we're not going to publish the transcript of a protected witness but here is a summary of what he said, the summary is not protected because what the Defence is arguing is it's only the literal transcript. So it would be the position of the OTP that whatever is in, it's the content, it's the subject of the closed-session testimony that is protected. And once the witness testifies and receives protection measures, a newspaper cannot print his witness statement if it covers the same material, they can't print a summary, they can't print any of that content or subject matter. Now, going back to the issue of identity. The -- it's very clear that Mr. Van Kuijk was awarded protection measures and it would be the OTP's position that therefore he is a protected witness, but that is an issue that needs clarification and it is something that you're going to have to decide, the difference between protection measures and a protected witness, because there are occasions where a witness's identity is not protected but the content of what he testifies to is protected. In this particular case it's very clear: The Blaskic Trial Chamber carefully considered arguments whether or not this witness should testify in closed session. In fact, they dedicated more or less an entire session to those arguments. Never at any time during that discussion did any of the Judges, did any of the Prosecution, did any of the Defence ever use Van Kuijk's name. There was no discussion that his name should be used, so it's very clear from the record that by their actions everyone in that courtroom was protecting his identity. And what's more, it can never be left to third parties to decide what was the real intent and parse out what is protected in closed-session testimony. It has to be a clear, simple principle that whatever is in closed session has to be protected. That would be the OTP's submission on the issue of identity. And then last, going to the 2000 order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, would your point be that the integrity of the protected testimony could be jeopardised if the witness testifying is not also protected, if the identity of the witness is not also protected? And would you be able to -- if that is your position, would you be able to identify any circumstances in which the disclosure of the witness's identity would jeopardise the security of the protected testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I think it would be our argument that if there is ambiguity in a record, in a transcript, that unless there is a clear expression that parties can use the witness's identity, that it has -- it has to be protected. In this particular case you don't have that because it's very clear the parties, by their actions, were protecting this witness. But if there is ever ambiguity -- for instance, here today where there was some ambiguity about the witness that we discussed, whether or not his identity was protected, we went into closed session. I think the position has to be a clear and simple one that unless the Chamber has clearly enunciated that you can use the witness's identity, that it has to be presumed to be protected because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I could think of another argument. My mind isn't made up on this issue, but one would start from the basic consideration that there's a right to a public trial, and that right is a fundamental human right and in accordance with generally accepted principles which have been set out by the European Court of Human Rights and other bodies. Any derogation from such a right must clearly be set out in a law, and the derogation must be proportionate to the -- to the particular measure that is being sought. Now, following that, I think it would -- it would contradict your argument that if there is any ambiguity, you would interpret the matter as favouring protection. I think that general principle would probably lead to the other conclusion, that if there is any ambiguity, you would interpret the matter as favouring publication because of the general right to a fair trial. And in that regard, it is significant that it is the Statute itself which authorises the derogation from the right to a public trial. The Statute itself authorises the Tribunal to make provisions for the protection of victims and witnesses, and one protective measure is closed session. So as I said, my mind isn't made up on it, there are arguments either way, but I would like you to take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I guess I should clarify when I say "ambiguity" in the record. If you have the situation where a witness testifies in closed session and his identity is never revealed in open session and the arguments were put forward only pertaining to the content of his testimony, you're now left with a situation with a newspaper gets that transcript, and what do you want them to do? Do you want them to go ahead and, because it was never clearly enunciated that his identity was protected, go ahead and publish that witness's identity in a newspaper, or is there a less extreme option that would be available to the newspaper, such as contacting the press office, the OTP spokesperson, an attorney at the OTP, somebody from Chambers who can refer somebody where they can make an application to the Court to find out whether or not his identity is protected. I agree with you that there is a compelling interest in having fair and public trials. The identity of a witness is only a small part of a public trial, but it also is counter-balanced by the difficulty in bringing witnesses into, as you're well aware from the Milosevic trial, very dangerous circumstances, oftentimes for their family and people they know, and for there to be a principle that a witness's identity can be revealed by a third party in the presumption that the identity is public unless stated to the contrary I think is very dangerous to these proceedings, and I think that the better principle should be that if anyone has some doubt about whether or not an identity is protected, they need to make application to the Court for a determination on that basis. I'm happy at this point now to go on to what would be the last submission, which is the 2000 order, unless Your Honours have any questions about the identity issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. We'll give the opportunity to briefly respond to the Defence. So please go on, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber in this case -- and I think it's clear from the transcript of Mr. Van Kuijk, that he's a protected witness. In 2000, the Blaskic Trial Chamber experienced two newspapers at that time who had published confidential information, and they issue the order for immediate cessation of violations of protective measures for witnesses, dated 1 December 2000. And it is specifically directed at those two newspapers, neither of which is Hrvatski List in this case. And the applicable provision is right after -- there is no page number in this order, unfortunately, but it's the second to last page. And if Your Honours can turn on the screen, we have a screen shot in Sanction that has the applicable provision of the order. And if I could ask you to direct your attention to the very last highlighted provision. The Blaskic Trial Chamber orders that: "The publication of statements or testimonies of the witness concerned, and generally of any protected witness, shall cease immediately ..." and states that: "Any publication of these statements or testimonies - statements or testimonies - shall expose its author(s) and those responsible to be found in contempt of the Tribunal ..." So there is a question, one, whether -- a factual question to be determined in this trial, whether or not the accused in this case had knowledge of this order, because Rule 77 requires that they knowingly violated this particular order, which we believe we can establish. And then secondly, by the terms of this order, does it apply to them? And we think it's very clear that if they have knowledge of it and they see this provision which says "the publication of statements or testimonies generally or of any protected witness must stop" clearly applies to what they did. And it would apply to both Mr. Marijacic and Mr. Rebic because it applies not only to the person who publishes but anyone else who is responsible and they clearly admit in the article that they're both participating in the decision. Mr. Rebic delivers the material, Mr. Marijacic publishes it, they do this hand-in-hand and cooperatively, so we think that this provision applies to both of them equally well. And that would be our legal submission on the application of the December 1, 2000 order. Of course it all stems from the closed session -- oral orders to move into closed session, right? It has to start with Van Kuijk as a protected witness, which the Appeals Chamber has ruled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it goes back to the closed-session order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, yes, the Appeals Chamber stated that this added nothing. Now, I wonder if they were considering this question, but that presupposes that they considered the closed-session order granted protection to witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: My interpretation of that provision in the Appeals Chamber order yesterday, we had asked them to lift the witness protections on Mr. Van Kuijk, and we cited the June 6, 1997 order, we cited the December 1, 2000 order, and we cited the oral orders in the transcript. They determined that the oral orders had protected him, and they lifted those, and then they looked at the December 1 order and had to determine did they need to do anything to modify the terms of that order in order to lift the protection on Mr. Van Kuijk. And I think what they're saying here is that once they lifted the protections that were granted in the oral orders of the transcript, he's no longer a protected witness. When he's no longer a protect witness, the December 1, 2000 order doesn't apply because it only applies to protected witnesses. So what we're saying here is when we lift the protected witness status of Mr. Van Kuijk, we don't have to do anything to the 2001 -- 2000 order because he is no longer a protected witness. That's my interpretation of that provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at page 4 of the Appeals Chamber's order, the first noting on that page says that: "Noting that in its order of 1st December, the Trial Chamber generally ordered that the publication of statements or testimonies of any protected witness in this case should cease immediately or otherwise be found in contempt of the International Tribunal but that the Trial Chamber did not grant any additional protective measures therein." Does that not presuppose that they understood the closed-session order to grant protection to the statements, or where else did they think that that protection came from?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have a moment? I want to just take a moment to review these passages again, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I've read the two provisions that you had referred to, and I think I agree with what you had stated, that they did presuppose that the closed-session testimony, as I had earlier submitted, protects the content of what the witness testified to, and that includes the statement if it covers the same material. That's exactly what they're saying here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akerson. And I wonder, the Prosecution has responded to the Defence allegation that either the closed session order or the order of this 1st of December, 2000, were not -- was not directly directed to these accused. Have you --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I will address that point, Your Honour. Thank you for bringing that to my attention. It would be our position that this -- if you can put the order back on the screen, if Your Honours have the December 1, 2000 order in front of you. The bottom provision is a general term. On its terms, it says publication of statements or testimonies of any protected witness, and states that any publication; not just the publication by those two newspapers but any publication. Now, what's key about this is not who it is directed at, because it's clearly directed very broadly. The key is who has knowledge of this order. And in this hearing we will -- the Prosecution will establish that these gentlemen would have had knowledge of this order and therefore it would apply to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akerson. I will hear briefly from the Defence on these issues. Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all I would like to refer to the last order the Prosecution invoked. I would like to stress its contents that has been quoted on a number of times here, which says that any publication must cease. I am interpreting this as read in Croatian, but I believe it's the same in English, French, and all the other official languages. It must cease. The text in the Hrvatski List newspaper was published three years later. That means that, ipso facto, this order cannot apply to this specific case. That is precisely what we have been trying to avoid all this time. We want to limit discussion in this case to the specific text that has been published. How can an order that was made by the Trial Chamber in the Blaskic case -- and the Prosecution provided us with a number of specific individual orders applying to various Croatian media, including Hrvatsko Slovo, Globus, Vjesnik, Vecernji List; all these are media in the Republic of Croatia. The Trial Chamber in the Blaskic case always issued specific individualised orders. In this specific case, there is not a single order referring or directed at Hrvatski List or Mr. Marijacic as its editor-in-chief. Therefore, extracting individual provisions from various orders without reading the whole order, without interpreting the spirit of the hearing in the Blaskic case is inappropriate, because the Trial Chamber in the Blaskic case always issued separate orders. The orders quoted by the Prosecution here do not refer to this protected witness we are discussing. They refer to the honour due to Trial Chambers' orders in other cases, other instances. Another issue: Why isn't Van Kuijk's name on the witness list? Whether he would have been a public, open witness or protected witness is another matter. There's no need to discuss it here. But he was not on the witness list. That is clearly a requirement. He was called as a witness as an afterthought. That's why his name is not even on his statement. Let me go back to the previous issue. In order for a violation of a Trial Chamber's order to exist, this violation must be wilful and knowing. How could Mr. Marijacic know about an order issued in a closed session? In the article that he published, there is no indication of protection or confidentiality or anything like that. His alleged culpability derives from another case, from another testimony, from a decision made by the Trial Chamber to apply to a different witness. We can move into private session to name that witness that I'm talking about so that everything could be absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ivanovic, I don't think we need to go into private session to name all those witnesses. Before that, Judge Bonomy has --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, this particular witness still enjoys protection. But if the Court doesn't mind, I can name them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Judge Bonomy has one question. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think we're listening to your whole argument at this stage, Mr. Ivanovic. We're just trying to understand what requires to be proved in the course of the trial. And one question I do have in that regard, the statement of the witness Van Kuijk, which you say hasn't -- his name doesn't appear on it at any place, I take it from your earlier submissions that your position is that what's available to the Trial Chamber as his statement is in fact a statement, and when you compare it with the transcript, they're different. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're not suggesting that there's any question over the authenticity of the statement. You accept the statement that exists, and you say, but the content of that wasn't published -- sorry, the content that was published was quite different from what was part of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is protected by the Trial Chamber's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You see, it seems to me the issues, as it has seemed to me for many months, that this case has endured is much simpler than any of the parties are prepared to concede, but I'm grateful for that concession. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, do you have anything further to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To begin with, I will say that I am completely in agreement with the judgement of Judge Bonomy. I was afraid to put it in so many words, but I have thought many times in this courtroom, Why are we wasting all this time when the matter is very clear? But I am familiar with the practice of this Tribunal, where I have worked as Defence counsel for five years, and I understand that we need to be cautious. If we let a piece of evidence slip, then it will reappear somewhere else. But the matters are very simple here: Where can the Prosecution find proof that Mr. Rebic disclosed the material to Mr. Marijacic? Second, if the Prosecution is adamant about claiming that it was done, what statement was that? What type of statement? Where was it given, and where did it come from, and where did they find the right to claim that it left the boundaries of this Tribunal? I don't know how the Prosecution will prove that, but I do know how much time will need to be wasted if they attempt to. Who says that this statement was not obtained through intelligence work on the ground in Central Bosnia and has nothing to do with the proceedings in this Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, that means that your case seems to be that the newspaper have published false material because they have a clear statement of a communication between Mr. Ivanovic and Mr. Rebic. Ivanovic is named as an editor-in-chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Marijacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Marijacic and Mr. Rebic. Marijacic is named as editor-in-chief and Rebic is named as a member of the board or editorial board of the magazine. Now, my tendency in a contempt case, I have to say, being a person who tends to apply common sense, is that that's on the face of it an indication of what happened, unless the two of you are at odds with each other. And that's what we're trying to find out, I think, at the moment before we embark on the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think there is a problem in communication, but in terms of common sense - and I thank you for supporting me in this - let us give it some thought. Do newspapers everywhere always publish only the truth, or are they pursuing sensationalist writing in order to make copy? Just a little patience, please. I'll respond. I only meant to stress where we are being led, I believe, by the Prosecution if they try to prove certain things. I was not trying to say that there was a problem in our internal communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I would like to finish. The sacred right of journalism and democracy that we as a young state are learning from you - and you see what has happened to us 15 years ago - is the right to inform the public. How will the Prosecution prove what statement that was, who gave it to the journalist, and whether the journalist is bound by a generally worded order? The order was made in a closed session concerning a closed session, and it will be very curious, once this Tribunal closes its doors, what lawyers will say, historians, legal institutes, if the Prosecution continues to view things in this manner. I do not think that this order can be linked with our case. It cannot be linked to any person outside the courtroom unless that person is acting knowingly and wilfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that concludes the legal submission in the first stage. And shall I deal with some housekeeping matters in relation to exhibits. On 13th of January, 2006, the Chamber issued a written decision on a Prosecution's motion for judicial notice and admission of evidence. By this decision, my understanding is that the Chamber admitted some 11 items into evidence prior to the commencement of the trial. If the Registry could please give the numbers to those items.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I shall be brief. I will just refer to the P numbers given by the OTP in their submission dated December and will allocate, if you kindly agree, a Registry number. The first number is referenced by OTP as P40, will get the number OTP number 1, with an English translation reference as OTP 1/E. The second exhibit number is referenced by OTP as P48, and will be allocated the reference number OTP 2, with an English translation referenced as OTP 2/E. The third exhibit is referenced by OTP as P9 and will be assigned the reference number OTP 3. There will be a B/C/S translation of this document referenced as OTP 3/B/C/S. The fourth exhibit number is referenced by OTP as P11 and will be assigned the reference OTP 4, with a B/C/S translation referenced as OTP 4/B/C/S. The fifth exhibit is mentioned by OTP as P13, 1-3, and will be assigned the reference OTP 5, with a B/C/S translation referenced as OTP 5/B/C/S. The sixth exhibit is referenced by OTP as P14 and will be allocated the reference number OTP 6. The seventh exhibit is referenced as P15 and will be referenced as OTP 7. Finally, the last exhibit is referenced by OTP as P37 and will be assigned the reference OTP 11, with a B/C/S translation referenced as OTP 11/B/C/S. This completes the list of exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And as for all the other documents, we will deal with their admission when it arises. And we come to the witnesses. Is it the Prosecution's position that they would lead all of the three witnesses as proposed?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We will only be calling two witnesses; Terry Cameron and William Tomljanovich.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll hear only the accused from the Defence. That wraps up the -- Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for me it depends on what we hear from Prosecution witnesses, rather, whether we will be calling the witnesses mentioned a moment ago. In the contrary case, I will gladly drop all my witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I just have one matter for the Pre-Trial Conference as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Which is that William Tomljanovich is going to be called as a witness in this case, and we would also like him to sit in the courtroom during the testimony of the accused, if they so choose to testify, because he is an expert of the documentation of Croatia and the archives of, in particular, Mr. Rebic, and it would be helpful for him to assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After he has testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: After he has testified, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that -- I'd like to hear from -- Mr. Krsnik has anything to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already had problems in other times where I acted as Defence counsel, with Mr. William Tomljanovich whose role was never quite clear to me nor was the position of the Prosecution, because the man is an historian. He now, as I see, appears as an investigator. In other case he's introduced as politician, a Ph.D. from Yale. In yet another case he appears for the Prosecution as an expert in a certain chapter of Croatian history. But as for this case today, I'm absolutely opposed to his presence in the courtroom apart from the time where he is testifying as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Marijacic absolutely subscribes to the position expressed by Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Rule 90(C) says: "A witness, other than an expert ... who has not yet testified shall not be present when the testimony of another witness is given." So I don't think Mr. Tomljanovich will be sitting before he gives testimony, and what the Defence has mentioned, it goes to the weight of the testimony of that witness. Unless Defence is able to identify specific reasons why he should not sit after he has given his testimony, I don't think there's any problem for Mr. Tomljanovich --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We must have misunderstood, because we thought he would be sitting in the courtroom, and that's the idea we are opposed to. We thought that after leaving the witness box, he would join the Prosecution on their bench, but if he's sitting at the gallery, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is the proposal. But what's actually wrong with that? They could have a secretary sitting beside them, helping them to work their way through the papers. What is the problem about a person who assists after he has given his evidence? That's what I don't understand at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he will be heard as a witness. That is as an independent party on the same matter, and then he will go on to assist the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Chamber would allow him to sit with the Prosecution after he has given his evidence. So for the sake of time saving, unless there's anything for the parties to raise during the Pre-Trial Conference, we'd like to go directly to the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I would just like to point out that we had prepared a ten-and-a-half minute opening statement which sets forth the factual grounds in this case. I would still prefer to go ahead and do the opening, but I understand the Court's concern and that you want to get right to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I announced we would not have opening statements but I would like to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view doing without it is enough. We can do it at closing argument. So please call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls witness Terrence Cameron. Terry Cameron. Your Honours, while the witness is coming into the Trial Chamber, we have prepared a demonstrative version of Exhibit P40, which is, I think, admitted Exhibit 1, which is the 18th of November edition. It just sets out the translation of text next to the actual pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Graham, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was just advised from the -- I was advised that -- [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are not hearing from the English booth. I think it's been corrected. I was advised from the technical booth we need to take a break right now to change the tape. So we'll break for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could take a seat. Ms. Graham.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Mr. Cameron, just before we begin I just want to inform you that yesterday evening the protective measures on Witness Van Kuijk were lifted, just so you know that we can refer to his name during the testimony. However, there may be other witnesses that you need to refer to, and those witnesses, if you could just refer to them as protected witness.

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to have distributed to the Court a demonstrative exhibit that we've prepared. It's a version of P40. If the usher could assist, that would be great. I'm also just passing out for Your Honours -- I've prepared just a list of the exhibits that I'm going to be dealing with during the testimony of this witness, just to assist for everyone to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. You may begin, Ms. Graham.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Witness, while this is being handed out, some preliminary questions for you. What is your work history?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: I was a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Canada's federal police force, for 25 years, retiring at the rank of staff sergeant. I immediately came to work for the OTP. I've been here as a senior investigator since June of 1998. During my service with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I conducted many, many interviews of suspects and witnesses, obtained witness statements, prepared trial briefs, testified in court. I had occasion to analyse many documents for most of my cases and submit reports based on those. During my service with the RCMP, or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I also served two tours with UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia. In 1992, I was station commander in Grubisno Polje in Croatia, and in 1994 I was station commander in Gorazde, Bosnia. During my time with the UN, I also had an opportunity to conduct investigations and interview witnesses in relation to crimes that had taken place in the former Yugoslavia. During my time at the Tribunal, I have travelled extensively to the former Yugoslavia and elsewhere, and during my duties conducted, again, many interviews, obtaining witness and suspect statements, collecting exhibits, analysis of documents, and reports based on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Witness, what was your role in the investigation related to Marijacic and Rebic?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: I was brought into this investigation on the 17th of December, 2004. I was briefed on the outline of the case, and I was asked to conduct an investigation and collect and analyse whatever relevant documents that I could find in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Witness, can you have a look at the demonstrative exhibit that you've been provided with.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is also visible on the computer evidence channel, if you'd like to view it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Witness, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: This document is a copy of the Hrvatski List article, or I should say publication, published on the 18th of November, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: And if I can identify it for the record, this is what has been identified as P40 and admitted as OTP Exhibit 1. Witness, does this edition of Hrvatski List identify on the cover the protected witness Van Kuijk?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Can you just quickly identify where he's named?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: On the top right-hand corner -- I'm sorry, the top left-hand corner. Part of it is hidden under the word "Tajni," and the second line down, I believe it is, is where the name would be, and you can see portions of that name. You can see the A, you can see the U and I.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Is it identified -- is he identified in any place outside the statement?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: Yes. If you look underneath the words "Carla Del Ponte," you will see at the bottom of that particular page where it says "Johan Van Kuijk" and "Ramal Goonewardene."

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, have you reviewed the statement that appears on the front of Hrvatski List?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: Yes, I have. The original statement was taken in English and translated into B/C/S by qualified translators of the OTP. I've made a comparison of the B/C/S version of the Van Kuijk statement with what is portrayed here on the front page of this article, of this publication.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: And can you confirm that portions of the statement are reproduced on this page?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Moving on to page 2 of the demonstrative exhibit, having looked at the cover --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before -- just before you do that, does it follow from what you've said that where it's claimed that on the 2nd of August the witness stated in his testimony before The Hague Tribunal that he had been approached two years previously by Bralo, that in fact that was not part of the transcript at the trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Witness, maybe I can clarify that for His Honour. The front page here refers to the testimony of Van Kuijk. Did Van Kuijk testify in August 1997?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: 2nd of August, I believe it was. I'm sorry, no. If I may refer to my statement, I can give a correct date for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Would Your Honour mind if the witness referred to his statement briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he can.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: If the usher would assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 16th of December, 1997 was the date that Mr. Van Kuijk actually testified at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Okay. From your review of documents, why has the -- has Hrvatski List referred to his testimony as being in August on the cover, which is of December?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
utterances.text: This is a representation of his witness statement and not his court transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean, then, that the issue of the surrender of Bralo didn't come up in the course of the trial, at least in the course of Van Kuijk's evidence in the trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not clear as to this matter. Are you saying that the witness statement says what is written here on the 2nd of August, 1997?

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can have the witness shown Exhibit P11, which is the statement of Witness Van Kuijk, and he can explain what is portrayed on the cover of the edition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just be clear that we need this evidence, or are you not going to present the documents and tell us in submissions what they say? The witness so far is causing confusion, but it's obviously a matter for you, but do we need this?

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just really wanted to deal with this demonstrative exhibit very briefly because Your Honour is correct, this is a matter for argument more than anything else. So maybe I'll leave the demonstrative exhibit there with the witness. We'll leave the front cover there with the witness and we can go on to the next subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Witness, as part of your investigation, have you reviewed editions of Slobodna Dalmacija?

utterances.speaker: TERRENCE CAMERON
